newsitem.title: USA: Canada aluminum association rules out new MOU.
newsitem.headline: Canada aluminum association rules out new MOU.

text.p: A new memorandum of understanding to curb aluminum production is a non-starter, but U.S. consumers are concerned about possible bids to bolster prices, North American aluminum industry sources said.
"The MOU was a good exercise but I don't think it is necessary any more," said Christian Van Houtte, president of the Quebec Aluminium Association.

"As far as we are concerned, Russian production is integrated into our system. It's up the whole international industry to decide what the supply will be - it's not for one country or one company to decide," Van Houtte added.

Russia's Konstern Alyuminiy chief executive Igor Prokopov said smelters had agreed to keep aluminum output at present levels. Some Russian smelters replied, however, they had no information about possible curbs.

Van Houtte meets Russian aluminum officials in Moscow this week, including Prokopov, as part of a two-year scheme to train Russian aluminum executives. Van Houtte said he would seek some clarification about the latest talking point.
LME three months aluminum settled at $1,328 a tonne Monday, near 2 and a 1/2 year lows, well below a peak of $2,195 in January 1994 during the MOU.

A Canadian diplomat said last week in Moscow that Russian and Canadian government officials had met to discuss curbing Russian output, rekindling memories of the Brussels Memorandum of Understanding between major aluminum producing countries of U.S., Russsia, Norway, Australia, and the European Union.
The U.S. Aluminum Association was unable to comment.
Van Houtte believed Canadian and Russian officials only met to discuss how to obtain production statistics from Russia's aluminum industry, and did not talk about production levels.

"As far as I know the only talks that took place were at the administrative level with civil servants asking one another will you send me your figures, and so on. It never went beyond that," Van Houtte said.
"If such talks took place (to curb output) - which I doubt, it was not done through the initiative of the Canadian Aluminium Association or its members."
The MOU set up a working group to publish production figures from each of the signatories. Publication ended earlier this year.
One trader familiar with Russian aluminum producers said Canadian and Russian officials undoubtedly met but he dismissed talk of another MOU.
"Russian production will remain stable. They would love to increase production but they have got no money," the trader added.

The MOU went into effect January 28, 1994 and lasted 24 months. In January this year a U.S. Trade Representative official told Reuters that the need for the MOU "has ended as far as we are concerned".
Another MOU with U.S. backing is almost certainly unlikely.

The MOU proved most problematic for the U.S. where consumers, arguing that post-MOU cuts by American producers were partly responsible for a rise in aluminum prices, prompted the Justice Dept to launch an anti-trust probe into the possibility of anti-competitive practices in the industry.
Some leading U.S. producers have already been advised by their legal counsel to avoid industry forums in case they could be construed to be talking to other producers.
U.S. federal offices were closed Monday for Columbus day.
Analyst Jim Southwood of Commodity Metals Management said the latest talk of possible curbs to Russian production has already sparked some jitters among U.S. consumers.

"Consumers, having been hurt by the rapid increase in prices that came from the first MOU are just kind of getting back to where they were before. They are wondering if that is going to happen all over again," Southwood said.

Southwood said the market is in much better shape than it was before the MOU was signed. "But having said that, at $1,300 a tonne, it is causing lots of people pain," Southwood said. "We cannot deny the fact that low prices are hurting the producers right now and it would be appropriate for them to do something about that."
Third quarter results at Alcoa and Kaiser Aluminum were hit by lower aluminum prices.
The U.S. majors, led by Alcoa, have some 800,000 tonnes of capcity shuttered, some idled during the MOU period.
